l: Heroic Age, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, The Ionic School
s: The Heroic Age ended with the conclusion of the Cycle and the death of Odysseus. The Cycle therefore brought the Greek epic history of the world down to the end of the heroic period.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, BIBLIOGRAPHY
s: This unit describes the manuscript traditions, papyrus evidence, editions, and scholarship concerning Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and the Epic Cycle. It lists manuscript witnesses and family groupings for the Works and Days, Theogony, Shield of Heracles, and Homeric Hymns, with particular attention to classifications by Rudolf Rzach and T. W. Allen. It also identifies papyrus fragments of Hesiodic works, especially the Catalogues, and surveys ancient, early modern, and modern editions and translations. The unit concludes with references for studying Hesiod, the Hesiodic poems, Greek literature, and the Epic Cycle.

l: Hesiod, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, BIBLIOGRAPHY
s: Hesiod is represented by manuscript and papyrus traditions for the Works and Days, Theogony, Shield of Heracles, and lost Hesiodic works. The unit lists editions, translations, fragments, and modern scholarship concerning Hesiod and his poems.

l: Homeric Hymns, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, BIBLIOGRAPHY
s: The Homeric Hymns are described as having a distinctly bad textual condition, with many defects, conjectural problems, and numerous lacunae. No papyrus fragment of the Hymns had emerged, although a papyrus contained a paraphrase closely parallel to the Hymn to Demeter.

l: Epic Cycle, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, BIBLIOGRAPHY
s: The fragments of the Epic Cycle derive from a variety of authors, so no single manuscript list is given. The unit names collections and editions by Muller, Dindorff, Kinkel, and Allen, and cites discussions by Welcker, Monro, and Croiset.

l: Works and Days, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, BIBLIOGRAPHY
s: The Works and Days is represented by one papyrus and numerous medieval manuscripts, which Rudolf Rzach divides into six families issuing from a common original. Papyrus evidence produced new lines at 169 a-d and improved readings at 278.

l: Theogony, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, BIBLIOGRAPHY
s: The Theogony is represented by papyri from the first century B.C. or first century A.D. through the fifth century and by medieval manuscripts. Rudolf Rzach divides the listed manuscripts into two main families, with the groups Ωa, Ωb, Ωc, and Ψ.

l: Catalogues, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, BIBLIOGRAPHY
s: The Catalogues are identified as the chief gain from the recovery of Hesiodic papyri. The unit lists papyrus fragments belonging to the lost Catalogues and assigns several of them to numbered fragments.

l: The Hesiodic Poems, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, BIBLIOGRAPHY
s: The Hesiodic poems are discussed through their papyrus and medieval manuscript evidence, modern editions, fragments, translations, and literary-historical studies. Recent work on them is reviewed by Rudolf Rzach in Bursian’s Jahresberichte.

l: Homer, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, BIBLIOGRAPHY
s: Homer is mentioned in connection with the early editions of the Homeric Hymns, the Epic Cycle, and related poems. Demetrius Chalcondyles’s 1488 edition included the Hymns, Epigrams, and Battle of the Frogs and Mice in the editio princeps of Homer.

l: Homeric Hymns manuscript tradition, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, BIBLIOGRAPHY
s: The Homeric Hymns manuscript tradition is represented by numerous medieval manuscripts enumerated by T. W. Allen. The manuscripts are traced to a common parent, from which three main families are derived, while M has a separate descent.

l: Rudolf Rzach, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, BIBLIOGRAPHY
s: Rudolf Rzach supplies the classification and numeration of the Works and Days manuscripts and divides them into families. He also divides the Theogony manuscripts into families, publishes major editions of Hesiod, and reviews recent work on the Hesiodic poems.

l: T. W. Allen, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, BIBLIOGRAPHY
s: T. W. Allen enumerates the medieval manuscripts of the Homeric Hymns and traces them to a common parent and three main families. He also wrote a discussion of the evidence for the date of Hesiod in the Journal of Hellenic Studies.

l: Demetrius Chalcondyles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, BIBLIOGRAPHY
s: Demetrius Chalcondyles produced an editio princeps of the Works and Days at Milan in 1493, or possibly 1493, and an edition of the Homeric Hymns at Florence in 1488. The latter also included the Epigrams and Battle of the Frogs and Mice.

l: Allen and Sikes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, BIBLIOGRAPHY
s: Allen and Sikes produced a 1904 London edition of the Homeric Hymns. The unit calls it by far the best edition, noting that it removes many conjectures and provides a valuable introduction and notes.

l: Oxyrhynchus Papyri, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, BIBLIOGRAPHY
s: The Oxyrhynchus Papyri provide witnesses for the Works and Days, Theogony, Shield of Heracles, and lost Hesiodic works. The unit specifically lists Oxyrhynchus Papyri 1090, 873, 689, 421, and 1358-9.

l: Hesiod manuscript tradition, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, BIBLIOGRAPHY
s: The Hesiod manuscript tradition includes papyri and medieval manuscripts for the Works and Days, Theogony, and Shield of Heracles. The recovery of Hesiodic papyri generally confirms the authority of the medieval manuscripts while also supplying new lines and improved readings.

l: Works and Days manuscripts, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, BIBLIOGRAPHY
s: The Works and Days manuscripts are designated S and A through Q and include witnesses from the fourth through fifteenth centuries, alongside the Oxyrhynchus Papyri witness. Rudolf Rzach groups them into Ωa, Ωb, Ψa, Ψb, Φa, and Φb.

l: Theogony manuscripts, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, BIBLIOGRAPHY
s: The Theogony manuscripts include papyri and medieval codices designated N, O, A through I, and K through L. Their families are Ωa = C,D; Ωb = E,F; Ωc = G,H,I; and Ψ = K,L.

l: Shield of Heracles manuscripts, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, BIBLIOGRAPHY
s: The Shield of Heracles manuscripts include papyrus witnesses and medieval manuscripts designated P, A, Q, and B through O. They belong chiefly to Ωa, Ωb, Ψa, and Ψb, with N and O additionally identified as mixed-family manuscripts.

l: Homeric Hymns manuscript families, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, BIBLIOGRAPHY
s: The Homeric Hymns manuscript families are identified as x1, x2, y, and p. T. W. Allen derives them from a common parent, with M excluded because it has a separate descent.

l: Aldine edition, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, BIBLIOGRAPHY
s: The Aldine edition of Hesiod was published at Venice in 1495 and contained the complete works. The Aldine edition of the Homeric Hymns was published at Venice in 1504.

l: Rzach editions of Hesiod, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, BIBLIOGRAPHY
s: Rzach’s editions of Hesiod include a larger Leipzig edition of 1902 and a smaller edition of 1913. The unit identifies these editions as important resources for Hesiodic poems and fragments.

l: Allen and Sikes edition, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, BIBLIOGRAPHY
s: The Allen and Sikes edition of the Homeric Hymns was published in London in 1904. It is praised for purging the text of conjectures and for the high value of its introduction and notes.

l: Greek literature, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, BIBLIOGRAPHY
s: The unit recommends the ordinary histories of Greek literature for the Hesiodic poems, especially the work of Croiset. It also notes that the summary account in Prof. Murray’s Ancient Greek Literature has a strong sceptical bias.

l: papyrus fragments, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, BIBLIOGRAPHY
s: Papyrus fragments confirm much of the authority of the medieval manuscripts and provide new lines, improved readings, and fragments of lost works. The most numerous and valuable discoveries concern the Catalogues.

l: medieval manuscripts, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, BIBLIOGRAPHY
s: Medieval manuscripts preserve the principal textual traditions of Hesiod and the Homeric Hymns. For Hesiod, papyrus discoveries generally confirm their authority; for the Homeric Hymns, T. W. Allen traces the listed medieval manuscripts to a common parent.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS
s: Hesiod addresses Perses about Zeus, justice, work, and the two forms of Strife, urging him to abandon violence and settle their inheritance dispute by right judgement. He recounts how Zeus hid the means of life, how Prometheus stole fire, and how Pandora was created as a punishment for mortals. He describes the successive races of mortal men, from the golden race to the present race of iron, and warns that Zeus punishes injustice. He concludes by instructing Perses about honest work, wealth, neighbors, reciprocity, and proper conduct.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS
s: Zeus gives or takes away strength, fame, and prosperity, and he straightens or destroys as he wills. He hides the means of life and fire, creates Pandora as a punishment for men, watches justice, and punishes violence and crooked judgement.

l: Perses, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS
s: Perses is urged to listen to right, reject violence, work diligently, and settle his inheritance dispute through true judgement. He is warned against idleness, dishonest gain, and taking another person's property.

l: Strife, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS
s: Strife has two forms: one promotes cruel war and battle, while the other is wholesome and drives people to work through rivalry. The beneficial Strife makes neighbors, craftsmen, beggars, and minstrels compete with one another.

l: Prometheus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS
s: Prometheus deceives Zeus and steals fire for men in a hollow fennel-stalk. His theft leads Zeus to plan sorrow and mischief for mankind.

l: fire, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS
s: Fire is hidden from men by Zeus and stolen by Prometheus for their use. Zeus calls it a great plague to Prometheus and men and makes Pandora the price for it.

l: Pandora, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS
s: Pandora is fashioned as a beautiful woman and given a deceitful nature, crafty words, and a shameless mind. She opens the jar and releases countless evils among men, while Hope remains inside.

l: gods, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS
s: The gods hide the means of life, create the races of mortal men, and punish mortals who fail to honor them. They also place the sweat of labor between men and Goodness.

l: men, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS
s: Mortal men receive right from Zeus, unlike beasts and birds, and are judged according to whether they practice justice or violence. They suffer toil, sickness, sorrow, and death, though honest work and right conduct can bring prosperity.

l: golden race, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS
s: The golden race lives during Cronos's reign like gods, free from sorrow, toil, grief, and old age. After death, its members become kindly spirits who guard mortal men and give wealth.

l: Silver Race, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS
s: The silver race is less noble than the golden race and remains childish for a hundred years. Its members become foolish and violent, fail to honor the gods, and are destroyed by Zeus.

l: brazen race, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS
s: The brazen race is strong, terrible, violent, and devoted to the works of Ares. Its members use bronze for armor, houses, and tools, and are destroyed by their own hands.

l: race of mortal men half-divine, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS
s: The race of heroes is nobler and more righteous than the brazen race and includes god-like demi-gods. War destroys some of them, while Zeus grants others a sorrow-free dwelling in the islands of the blessed.

l: Iron Age, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS
s: The race of iron is marked by unending labor, sorrow, conflict, dishonor, envy, and the triumph of strength over right. Zeus will destroy it when its corruption becomes complete.

l: Justice, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS
s: Justice is the daughter of Zeus and is honored among the gods. She reports human wrongdoing to Zeus, leaves cities that reject her, and brings prosperity to those who give straight judgements.

l: princes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS
s: Princes are warned that the gods watch them and that whole cities may suffer for their crooked judgements. They are told to make their judgements straight and reject bribes.

l: city, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS
s: A city that gives straight judgements flourishes, while one ruled by violence and crooked judgement suffers famine, plague, war, and destruction. Justice and Peace support the prosperous city.

l: Righteousness, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS
s: Right is given to mankind by Zeus and is better than the law governing beasts, fishes, and birds. Those who know and speak right may receive prosperity, while false witnesses bring ruin upon their generations.

l: violence, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS
s: Violence is condemned as harmful to both poor and prosperous men. Zeus punishes those who practice it, while Justice eventually defeats Outrage.

l: work, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS
s: Work is presented as honorable, necessary, and the path to wealth and the favor of the gods. Properly ordered work fills barns with food and protects people from hunger.

l: hunger, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS
s: Hunger is described as the fitting companion of the sluggard. Work keeps hunger away, while idleness leaves a person in need.

l: wealth, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS
s: God-given wealth is better than wealth gained through violence, theft, or deceit. Wealth acquired wrongly is temporary, while honest work and careful increase preserve it.

l: inheritance dispute, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS
s: The inheritance dispute concerns Perses taking a greater share and bribing or influencing lords who judge the case. Hesiod urges that the dispute be settled with true judgement and warns that Perses must not repeat such conduct.

l: judgement, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS
s: Judgement must be straight, truthful, and free from bribes. Crooked judgement harms the city and brings punishment from Zeus, while fair judgement brings peace and prosperity.

l: war, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS
s: War is associated with the harmful form of Strife, violence, and the destruction of mortal races. It destroys parts of the race of heroes and may be sent by Zeus against unjust cities.

l: Pandora's creation, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HESIOD / HESIOD’S WORKS AND DAYS
s: Pandora's creation is ordered by Zeus after Prometheus steals fire. Hephaestus forms her from earth and water, while Athene, Aphrodite, Hermes, the Graces, Persuasion, and the Hours provide her clothing, beauty, speech, and deceptive qualities.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 370-372) Let the wage promised to a friend be fixed; even with
s: The passage advises fixing a wage promised to a friend and getting a witness, even when dealing with a brother, because trust and mistrust can ruin men. It warns that a flaunting woman may coax, deceive, and seek a man’s barn, and it calls womankind deceptive. It recommends an only son to feed his father’s house, while saying that leaving a second son means dying old; Zeus can nevertheless grant great wealth to many. Those who desire wealth are told to work with work upon work.

l: trust, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 370-372) Let the wage promised to a friend be fixed; even with
s: Trust, like mistrust, ruins men. A promised wage should be fixed and witnessed even when it concerns a friend or brother.

l: mistrust, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 370-372) Let the wage promised to a friend be fixed; even with
s: Mistrust, like trust, ruins men. A witness should be obtained when fixing a promised wage.

l: flaunting woman, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 370-372) Let the wage promised to a friend be fixed; even with
s: The flaunting woman may coax, cozen, and deceive a man because she is after his barn.

l: womankind, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 370-372) Let the wage promised to a friend be fixed; even with
s: Womankind is described as deceptive to the man who trusts it.

l: only son, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 370-372) Let the wage promised to a friend be fixed; even with
s: The only son should feed his father’s house, so that wealth will increase in the home.

l: second son, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 370-372) Let the wage promised to a friend be fixed; even with
s: If a man leaves a second son, he should die old.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 370-372) Let the wage promised to a friend be fixed; even with
s: Zeus can easily give great wealth to a greater number.

l: wealth, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 370-372) Let the wage promised to a friend be fixed; even with
s: Wealth increases in the home when an only son feeds his father’s house. A person who desires wealth is told to work with work upon work.

l: work, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 370-372) Let the wage promised to a friend be fixed; even with
s: More hands mean more work and more increase. A person who desires wealth is told to undertake work upon work.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 383-404) When the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas, are rising 1310,
s: The unit gives Perses a calendar of agricultural labor, advising him when to plough, sow, harvest, cut timber, prune vines, and store produce. It instructs him to prepare a house, ploughs, oxen, slaves, tools, clothing, fodder, and provisions before each season. Zeus, Demeter, and other gods are invoked as powers affecting crops, rain, and human livelihood. The passage warns that idleness, unpaid debts, and poor preparation may bring Perses and his household to hunger and dependence on neighbors.

l: Perses, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 383-404) When the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas, are rising 1310,
s: Perses is urged to work according to the seasons, pay his debts, and avoid hunger. He is told to prepare a house, a woman, an ox, ploughs, slaves, tools, and provisions, and to carry out ploughing, sowing, harvesting, and storage at the proper times.

l: Pleiades, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 383-404) When the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas, are rising 1310,
s: The Pleiades signal the seasons of agricultural work. Their rising marks the beginning of harvest, their setting marks ploughing, and their reappearance after forty nights and days indicates when the sickle should be sharpened; when they climb up the plants, vineyard digging should cease.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 383-404) When the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas, are rising 1310,
s: Zeus sends autumn rains and may give a good result to ploughing and crops. Zeus of the Earth is invoked, together with Demeter, to make the grain sound and heavy, and his will is said to vary at different times.

l: Demeter, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 383-404) When the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas, are rising 1310,
s: Demeter’s fruits and holy grain are to be produced through timely labor. She is invoked with Zeus of the Earth to make the grain sound and heavy.

l: Sirius, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 383-404) When the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas, are rising 1310,
s: Sirius passes over the heads of men for a short time by day and takes a greater share of night as autumn approaches. Later, Sirius parches the head and knees and makes the skin dry during the season of intense heat.

l: gods, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 383-404) When the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas, are rising 1310,
s: The gods have ordained work for men. The passage presents seasonal labor as necessary for avoiding want and securing a livelihood.

l: men, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 383-404) When the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas, are rising 1310,
s: Men must plough, sow, harvest, prepare tools, store grain, and adapt their work to weather and seasonal signs. Men who are idle, late, or dependent on others risk hunger, while those who work diligently may have plenty and help others.

l: the slaves, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 383-404) When the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas, are rising 1310,
s: Slaves are assigned agricultural and household work, including following the oxen, scattering seed, hiding seed from birds, harvesting, winnowing grain, and carrying out commands. They are to work in wet and dry conditions during the ploughing season, and in midsummer they are told to build barns.

l: oxen, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 383-404) When the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas, are rising 1310,
s: Two nine-year-old oxen are recommended for ploughing because their strength is unspent and they are in their prime. They should be fed in the byre before ploughing, given half their usual food in winter, and allowed to rest after work.

l: agricultural labor and seasonal work, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 383-404) When the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas, are rising 1310,
s: Agricultural labor must follow seasonal signs, including the rising and setting of the Pleiades, the crane’s call, the cuckoo’s call, and the appearances of Arcturus, the swallow, Orion, and Sirius. The work includes ploughing, sowing, pruning, harvesting, winnowing, storing grain, cutting timber, and tending vines and animals.

l: debts and hunger, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 383-404) When the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas, are rising 1310,
s: Perses is warned to find a way to pay his debts and avoid hunger. If he delays work and must seek help from neighbors, they may refuse him after he has asked repeatedly.

l: house, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 383-404) When the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas, are rising 1310,
s: A house is listed among the first necessities, together with a woman and an ox for the plough. It should be prepared with supplies and barns so that work will not depend on another person’s assistance.

l: the plough, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 383-404) When the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas, are rising 1310,
s: Two ploughs should be prepared at home, one made all of a piece and one jointed, so that one can replace the other if it breaks. Their parts should be made from suitable woods, including laurel, elm, oak, and holm-oak.

l: grain and crops, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 383-404) When the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas, are rising 1310,
s: Grain should be sown when the soil is ready and guarded from birds. It is to be winnowed on a smooth threshing-floor, measured, stored in jars, and kept safely indoors.

l: harvest, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 383-404) When the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas, are rising 1310,
s: Harvest begins when the Pleiades rise, and the sickle should be sharpened at the proper seasonal time. Workers are told to rise early, bring the fruits home, and later cut grape-clusters, expose them to the sun, cover them, and draw off the wine.

l: winter, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 383-404) When the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas, are rising 1310,
s: Winter brings frost, cold winds, snow, rain, and difficult conditions for sheep and men. People should prepare clothing, footwear, shelter, barns, and fodder beforehand, work before the dark clouds arrive, and give men more food while giving oxen half their usual food.

l: spring, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 383-404) When the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas, are rising 1310,
s: Grey spring returns after winter, when Earth again bears varied fruit. The swallow’s appearance signals the beginning of spring, and fallow land may be ploughed while the soil is becoming light.

l: rain, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 383-404) When the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas, are rising 1310,
s: Autumn rain makes men’s bodies feel easier and marks a season for cutting timber. Rain can also rescue late ploughing if Zeus sends it on the third day and it reaches the proper depth without exceeding an ox’s hoof.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 618-640) But if desire for uncomfortable sea-faring seize you;
s: The speaker instructs Perses about seasonal sailing, farming, trade, household conduct, religious purity, and auspicious days. He warns that autumn storms make the sea dangerous, recommends sailing fifty days after the solstice or cautiously in spring, and advises limiting cargo to avoid disaster. He recounts that their father sailed from Aeolian Cyme to escape poverty and settled near Helicon, while the speaker claims little sailing experience but authority from the Muses and Zeus. The unit concludes with rules for marriage, friendship, ritual behavior, bodily cleanliness, and the proper days for different kinds of work.

l: Perses, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 618-640) But if desire for uncomfortable sea-faring seize you;
s: Perses is told to remember that all works have their season, especially sailing. He is advised about safe sailing times, limited cargo, marriage, friendship, ritual purity, social conduct, and the proper days for work.

l: Hesiod, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 618-640) But if desire for uncomfortable sea-faring seize you;
s: The speaker claims little experience of sea-faring, having sailed only from Aulis to Euboea, where he won a song contest at Chalcis and dedicated a tripod to the Muses of Helicon. He nevertheless says that the Muses taught him to sing and that he can declare the will of Zeus.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 618-640) But if desire for uncomfortable sea-faring seize you;
s: Zeus sends poverty upon men and governs the days that are to be observed for work. The speaker says that the outcomes of good and evil at sea rest with Zeus and Poseidon, and that Zeus sends autumn rain and storms.

l: sea, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 618-640) But if desire for uncomfortable sea-faring seize you;
s: The sea becomes dangerous when the Pleiades plunge into it and autumn storms arise. It is relatively harmless fifty days after the solstice, passable in spring, and a place where men risk death when they sail in ignorance or overload their ships.

l: sea-faring and sailing, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 618-640) But if desire for uncomfortable sea-faring seize you;
s: Sailing should be avoided when the Pleiades descend and winter gales begin. The best stated time for sailing is fifty days after the solstice, while spring sailing is possible but dangerous; sailors should return before the new wine, autumn rain, and storms of Notus.

l: the ship, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 618-640) But if desire for uncomfortable sea-faring seize you;
s: A ship should be hauled onto land, packed around with stones, drained through its bilge-plug, and protected from rain. Its tackle and fittings should be stored in the house, its wings stowed, and its rudder hung over the smoke; cargo should be kept within a safe measure.

l: destructive winds, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 618-640) But if desire for uncomfortable sea-faring seize you;
s: Gales of many kinds rage when the Pleiades escape Orion's strength. Notus accompanies Zeus's heavy autumn rain, stirs the sea, and makes the deep dangerous, whereas the winds are steady and favorable fifty days after the solstice.

l: agricultural labor and seasonal work, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 618-640) But if desire for uncomfortable sea-faring seize you;
s: When sailing is unsafe, the speaker tells Perses to till the land. He gives seasonal and calendar guidance for sowing, planting, reaping, shearing sheep, cutting timber, building ships, opening wine-jars, and putting yokes on animals.

l: riches and wealth, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 618-640) But if desire for uncomfortable sea-faring seize you;
s: If Perses turns to trading to escape debt and hunger, the speaker advises placing freight in a large ship because greater lading can bring greater profit if the winds remain favorable. He also warns against risking all one's goods at sea.

l: marriage and household, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 618-640) But if desire for uncomfortable sea-faring seize you;
s: A man should marry when he is near thirty, choosing a grown woman who has been raised for four years and lives nearby. He should marry a maiden so that he can teach her careful ways, since a good wife is the greatest household gain and a bad, greedy wife brings misery and old age.

l: friendship and social conduct, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 618-640) But if desire for uncomfortable sea-faring seize you;
s: A friend should not be treated exactly like a brother unless he is treated justly, and a wrong should be repaid double if the offender refuses reconciliation. Perses is told to avoid shifting friendships, lavishness, churlishness, rogues, slander, boasting, taunting the poor, boorishness at feasts, and harmful talk.

l: ritual purity and religious observance, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 618-640) But if desire for uncomfortable sea-faring seize you;
s: The speaker forbids making libations with unwashed hands, crossing rivers without washing, mocking sacrifices, polluting rivers and springs, and using uncharmed pots. He also gives rules about bodily cleanliness, burial, childbirth, exposure, urination, and cutting plants at a festival, warning that the gods punish ritual offenses.

l: the calendar and auspicious days, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 618-640) But if desire for uncomfortable sea-faring seize you;
s: The thirtieth day is recommended for reviewing work and distributing supplies, while the first, fourth, seventh, eighth, ninth, eleventh, and twelfth have various favorable uses. Other days are assigned to planting, sowing, births, marriage, gelding animals, building ships, opening jars, yoking animals, and hauling ships, while fifth days and several others are declared unfavorable or changeable.

l: gods, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 618-640) But if desire for uncomfortable sea-faring seize you;
s: The gods govern omens, sacred days, fortune, and the consequences of ritual violations. The speaker says that people should pray, observe purity, avoid offending the deathless gods, and discern the omens of birds.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE DIVINATION BY BIRDS
s: The unit concerns the work titled The Divination by Birds and its placement relative to Works and Days. Proclus states that some people place The Divination by Birds after verse 828 of Works and Days. Apollonius of Rhodes rejects The Divination by Birds as spurious.

l: The Divination by Birds, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE DIVINATION BY BIRDS
s: The Divination by Birds is placed by some after verse 828 of Works and Days. Apollonius of Rhodes rejects it as spurious.

l: Proclus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE DIVINATION BY BIRDS
s: Proclus discusses The Divination by Birds in relation to verse 828 of Works and Days.

l: Works and Days, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE DIVINATION BY BIRDS
s: Verse 828 of Works and Days is identified as the verse after which some place The Divination by Birds.

l: Apollonius Rhodius, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE DIVINATION BY BIRDS
s: Apollonius of Rhodes rejects The Divination by Birds as spurious.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE ASTRONOMY
s: The Astronomy, attributed to Hesiod, discusses the Pleiades and Hyades and gives their names and star-related traditions. It recounts how Callisto became the Great Bear and how her son Arcas became Bootes. It also tells of Orion, his parentage, adventures, death by a scorpion, and placement among the stars, along with the scorpion. Hesiod further says that Orion piled up the promontory by Peloris, founded a close of Poseidon, settled in Euboea, and was honored among the stars.

l: The Astronomy, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE ASTRONOMY
s: The Astronomy, attributed to Hesiod, calls the Pleiades Peleiades and refers to their setting and disappearance. It also contains accounts of the Hyades, Callisto and the Great Bear, and Orion.

l: Hesiod, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE ASTRONOMY
s: Hesiod is credited with The Astronomy and with accounts of the Pleiades, Hyades, Callisto, Arcas, and Orion. He says that Lycaon entertained Zeus and served him the babe he had cut up, and that Orion piled up the promontory by Peloris and founded the close of Poseidon.

l: Pleiades, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE ASTRONOMY
s: The Pleiades are called Peleiades in The Astronomy, although mortals call them Pleiades. They are described as stormy and as going down or hiding away.

l: Hyades, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE ASTRONOMY
s: The Hyades are identified as the transformed sisters of Hyas. Hesiod gives their names as Phaesyle, Coronis, Cleeia, Phaco, and Eudora, and says that people on earth call them Hyades.

l: Great Bear, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE ASTRONOMY
s: The Great Bear is identified with Callisto, the daughter of Lycaon. Zeus placed her among the stars and gave her the name Bear because of her misfortune.

l: Callisto, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE ASTRONOMY
s: Callisto was the daughter of Lycaon and lived in Arcadia, occupying herself with wild beasts in the mountains with Artemis. Zeus seduced her, and after Artemis discovered that she was pregnant, Artemis changed her into a bear; Callisto later gave birth to Arcas and was placed among the stars by Zeus.

l: Lycaon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE ASTRONOMY
s: Lycaon was Callisto's father. He received Callisto and her babe after goat-herds gave them up to him, and, according to Hesiod, entertained Zeus while pretending not to know what had happened and served him the cut-up babe.

l: Artemis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE ASTRONOMY
s: Artemis accompanied Callisto in hunting wild beasts in the mountains. After seeing Callisto bathing while pregnant, she became enraged and changed Callisto into a bear; she later prayed with Leto for Orion.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE ASTRONOMY
s: Zeus seduced Callisto and fathered Arcas. He delivered Callisto from being killed by her son and the Arcadians, then placed her among the stars as the Great Bear; he also placed Orion among the stars after Artemis and Leto prayed for him.

l: Arcas, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE ASTRONOMY
s: Arcas was the son of Callisto and Zeus. He was given up with his mother to Lycaon, later pursued her with the Arcadians, and is identified as Bootes, the Bear-warden.

l: Orion, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE ASTRONOMY
s: Orion was the son of Euryale, daughter of Minos, and Poseidon, and could walk on the waves as on land. After outraging Merope, being blinded by Oenopion, and being healed in the east, he hunted with Artemis and Leto in Crete, was killed by a scorpion sent by Earth, and was placed among the stars by Zeus; Hesiod also says that he settled in Euboea and was remembered among the stars.

l: Poseidon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE ASTRONOMY
s: Poseidon was the father of Orion with Euryale, the daughter of Minos. Orion also founded a close of Poseidon by the promontory of Peloris, according to Hesiod.

l: Oenopion, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE ASTRONOMY
s: Oenopion was the father of Merope. After Orion outraged Merope while drunk, Oenopion had Orion blinded and expelled from the country, and later hid underground when Orion returned seeking punishment.

l: scorpion, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE ASTRONOMY
s: The scorpion was a very large creature sent up by Earth after Orion threatened to kill every beast on earth. It stung and killed Orion, and Zeus placed it among the stars as a memorial of what had occurred.

l: Orion’s transformation into a constellation, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE ASTRONOMY
s: After Orion was killed by the scorpion, Zeus placed him among the stars at the request of Artemis and Leto because of his manliness. Hesiod also says that Orion was taken into the number of the stars after settling in Euboea.

l: Orion and the scorpion among the stars, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE ASTRONOMY
s: Zeus placed both Orion and the scorpion among the stars. The scorpion was set there as a memorial of Orion and of the events that led to his death.

l: Orion’s death, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE ASTRONOMY
s: Orion died after Earth sent a very large scorpion against him because he threatened to kill every beast on earth. The scorpion stung him, after which Zeus placed Orion among the stars.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE PRECEPTS OF CHIRON
s: The Precepts of Chiron contains advice to offer sacrifices to the eternal gods upon returning home and to hear both sides before deciding a suit. It also preserves a sequence comparing the lifespans of crows, stags, ravens, phoenixes, and the rich-haired Nymphs. Quintilian reports that earlier writers attributed the work to Hesiod and that Aristophanes was the first to reject it as Hesiod's work. The unit presents no further information about Chiron beyond the work's title.

l: The Precepts of Chiron, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE PRECEPTS OF CHIRON
s: The Precepts of Chiron contains precepts about sacrificing to the eternal gods upon returning home and hearing both sides before deciding a suit. It also includes a lifespan comparison involving crows, stags, ravens, phoenixes, and the rich-haired Nymphs. Earlier writers attributed it to Hesiod, but Aristophanes was the first to reject it as a work of Hesiod.

l: Chiron, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE PRECEPTS OF CHIRON
s: Chiron is named in the title The Precepts of Chiron, but the unit provides no other information about him.

l: Hesiod, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE PRECEPTS OF CHIRON
s: Many writers earlier than Aristophanes attributed The Precepts of Chiron to Hesiod. Quintilian reports that Aristophanes was the first to reject the work as Hesiod's.

l: Aristophanes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE PRECEPTS OF CHIRON
s: Aristophanes was the first, according to Quintilian, to reject The Precepts of Chiron as a work of Hesiod.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE GREAT WORKS
s: The Great Works is cited in a commentary on Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics for a verse about the slaying of Rhadamanthys. The verse states that a person who sows evil will reap an increased evil, and that receiving treatment matching one’s own actions constitutes true justice. Proclus reports that some people attribute the Silver Race to the earth because Hesiod identifies silver as belonging to the family of Earth in the Great Works.

l: Great Works, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE GREAT WORKS
s: The Great Works contains a verse about the slaying of Rhadamanthys, stating that evil deeds bring an increased evil harvest and that reciprocal treatment is true justice. It is also cited as the work in which Hesiod makes silver part of the family of Earth.

l: Hesiod, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE GREAT WORKS
s: Hesiod is credited with the Great Works, which contains the verse about the slaying of Rhadamanthys. According to Proclus, Hesiod makes silver belong to the family of Earth in that work.

l: Silver Race, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE GREAT WORKS
s: Some people attribute the Silver Race to the earth. This attribution is based on the claim that Hesiod makes silver part of the family of Earth in the Great Works.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE IDAEAN DACTYLS
s: Hesiod says that the Idaean Dactyls taught the smelting and tempering of iron in Crete. Clement reports that Celmis and Damnameneus, identified as the first Idaean Dactyls, discovered iron in Cyprus. Clement also says that Delas discovered bronze smelting, while Hesiod calls him Scythes.

l: Idaean Dactyls, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE IDAEAN DACTYLS
s: The Idaean Dactyls are said by Hesiod to have taught the smelting and tempering of iron in Crete. Celmis and Damnameneus are identified as the first of them.

l: Celmis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE IDAEAN DACTYLS
s: Celmis is identified as one of the first Idaean Dactyls. He is said by Clement to have discovered iron in Cyprus.

l: Damnameneus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE IDAEAN DACTYLS
s: Damnameneus is identified as one of the first Idaean Dactyls. He is said by Clement to have discovered iron in Cyprus.

l: Delas, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE IDAEAN DACTYLS
s: Delas is identified as an Idaean who discovered bronze smelting.

l: Scythes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE IDAEAN DACTYLS
s: Scythes is the name Hesiod gives to Delas.

l: iron, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE IDAEAN DACTYLS
s: Iron was discovered in Cyprus by Celmis and Damnameneus, according to Clement. Hesiod says that the Idaean Dactyls taught its smelting and tempering in Crete.

l: bronze, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE IDAEAN DACTYLS
s: Bronze smelting was discovered by Delas, according to Clement.

l: tempering of iron, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE IDAEAN DACTYLS
s: Hesiod says that the Idaean Dactyls taught the tempering of iron in Crete.

l: discovery of iron, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE IDAEAN DACTYLS
s: The discovery of iron in Cyprus is attributed by Clement to Celmis and Damnameneus, the first Idaean Dactyls.

l: bronze smelting, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE IDAEAN DACTYLS
s: Bronze smelting was discovered by Delas, whom Hesiod calls Scythes.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEOGONY
s: The Muses of Helicon inspire Hesiod to sing of the gods and their origins, declaring that they can speak both falsehoods and truths. The divine genealogy begins with Chaos, Earth, Tartarus, and Eros, then recounts the births of Heaven, the Titans, the Cyclopes, and the Hundred-Handed Ones. Earth helps Cronos overthrow Heaven with a sickle, after which many divine beings and monsters are born from the gods. The unit also describes the Muses, Zeus's rise to power, and Styx's alliance with him against the Titans.

l: Hesiod, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEOGONY
s: Hesiod was shepherding his lambs under holy Helicon when the Muses taught him glorious song. They gave him a laurel rod, breathed a divine voice into him, and instructed him to sing of the gods.

l: Muses, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEOGONY
s: The Muses of Helicon dwell on the holy mount, dance near its springs, and sing of Zeus, the gods, and the race of immortals. They told Hesiod that they know how to speak many false things as though they were true, but can utter true things when they choose.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEOGONY
s: Zeus is praised as the aegis-holder, father of gods and men, and supreme in power. After overcoming Cronos, he ruled in heaven, distributed portions and privileges among the immortals, and promised offices and rights to gods who fought against the Titans.

l: Aphrodite, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEOGONY
s: Aphrodite is called a lovely goddess born from sea foam. Eros and Desire accompanied her, and she received the portion of whisperings, smiles, deceits, love, and graciousness among gods and mortals.

l: Cronos, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEOGONY
s: Cronos was the youngest and most terrible of Earth and Heaven's children, and he hated his father. At Earth's urging, he used a jagged sickle to cut off Heaven's members and later ruled until Zeus overcame him.

l: Earth, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEOGONY
s: Earth was one of the first beings to come into existence and became the sure foundation of the immortals. She bore Heaven, the hills, Pontus, the Titans, the Cyclopes, and the Hundred-Handed Ones, and she aided Cronos in attacking Heaven.

l: Oceanus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEOGONY
s: Oceanus was one of the Titans born from Earth and Heaven. With Tethys he fathered rivers and a vast number of daughters who serve the earth and deep waters.

l: Night, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEOGONY
s: Night arose from Chaos and gave birth to Aether and Day through union with Erebus. Without lying with anyone, she also bore Doom, Fate, Death, Sleep, Dreams, Blame, Woe, the Hesperides, the Destinies, Nemesis, Deceit, Friendship, Age, and Strife.

l: Heaven, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEOGONY
s: Heaven was born from Earth as her equal and covered her as the dwelling-place of the blessed gods. He fathered the Titans, Cyclopes, and Hundred-Handed Ones with Earth, hid his children away, and was mutilated by Cronos.

l: Olympus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEOGONY
s: Olympus is the home of Zeus, the Muses, and the immortals. The Muses sing there, Zeus called the deathless gods there before fighting the Titans, and Styx came there first with her children to support him.

l: Mnemosyne, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEOGONY
s: Mnemosyne, who reigns over the hills of Eleuther, bore nine daughters to Zeus after nine nights of union. These daughters are the Muses, whose songs bring forgetfulness of ills and rest from sorrow.

l: Chaos, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEOGONY
s: Chaos was the first being to come into existence. Erebus and black Night came forth from Chaos.

l: Tartarus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEOGONY
s: Tartarus came into existence near the beginning, alongside Chaos, Earth, and Eros. It lies in the depth of wide-pathed Earth.

l: Eros, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEOGONY
s: Eros was one of the first deathless gods to come into existence and was called fairest among them. He unnerves the limbs and overcomes the minds and wise counsels of gods and men.

l: Titans, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEOGONY
s: The Titans were born from Earth and Heaven. Heaven called them Titans in reproach because they strained and committed a fearful deed when Cronos attacked him.

l: Cyclopes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEOGONY
s: The Cyclopes Brontes, Steropes, and Arges were born from Earth and Heaven. They had one eye in the middle of each forehead and later gave Zeus the thunder and made the thunderbolt.

l: Aphrodite's birth, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEOGONY
s: After Cronos cut off Heaven's members and cast them into the sea, foam formed around the immortal flesh and a maiden grew within it. She approached Cythera and then Cyprus, where she emerged as Aphrodite.

l: Medusa, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEOGONY
s: Medusa was one of the Gorgons born to Ceto and Phorcys and was mortal, unlike her two sisters. After Perseus cut off her head, Chrysaor and Pegasus sprang from her.

l: Styx, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEOGONY
s: Styx, the chiefest of Ocean and Tethys's daughters, joined with Pallas and bore Zelus, Nike, Cratos, and Bia. She came first to Olympus with her children to support Zeus against the Titans, and Zeus made her the great oath of the gods.

l: Theogony, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEOGONY
s: The theogony is presented as a song about the race of the blessed gods, beginning with their origins and continuing through their births, honors, and divisions of power. The Muses are asked to tell which beings first came to be and how the gods took Olympus.

l: divine song, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEOGONY
s: Divine song is taught by the Muses and celebrates things that were, are, and will be. It honors gods and ancient men, gives princes persuasive speech, and relieves sorrow when a singer chants the glorious deeds of the past.

l: divine genealogy, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEOGONY
s: The divine genealogy traces the immortals from Chaos, Earth, Tartarus, and Eros through the births of the Titans, Olympians, rivers, goddesses, and monsters. It also records how the gods divided honors and how Zeus came to rule.

l: sickle, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE THEOGONY
s: Earth made a great sickle from grey flint and placed it in Cronos's hands. Cronos used the jagged sickle to cut off Heaven's members during an ambush.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 404-452) Again, Phoebe came to the desired embrace of Coeus.
s: Phoebe and Coeus beget Leto, Asteria, and Hecate. Zeus honours Hecate above all and preserves her original share in earth, heaven, and sea. Hecate grants favour, wealth, victory, glory, success in contests, prosperity in herds, and abundant catches at sea to those she chooses. Zeus also makes her a nurse of the young who see the light of Dawn.

l: Hecate, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 404-452) Again, Phoebe came to the desired embrace of Coeus.
s: Hecate is born to Phoebe and Coeus and is honoured by Zeus above all. She retains privilege in earth, heaven, and sea, and aids or advances whom she chooses in judgment, assemblies, battle, games, horsemanship, seafaring, and the keeping of herds. Zeus makes her a nurse of the young who later see the light of Dawn.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 404-452) Again, Phoebe came to the desired embrace of Coeus.
s: Zeus honours Hecate above all and gives her splendid gifts. He does not take away any part of her original portion among the former Titan gods, and he makes her a nurse of the young.

l: gods, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 404-452) Again, Phoebe came to the desired embrace of Coeus.
s: Hecate is honoured exceedingly by the deathless gods. She is said to have a share among them in honour, as well as in earth, heaven, and sea.

l: division of Hecate's portion, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 404-452) Again, Phoebe came to the desired embrace of Coeus.
s: Hecate's portion was divided at the first from the beginning among earth, heaven, and sea. Zeus preserves all of this portion for her and takes nothing away.

l: sacrifices and prayers, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 404-452) Again, Phoebe came to the desired embrace of Coeus.
s: When people on earth offer rich sacrifices and pray according to custom, they call upon Hecate for favour. When she receives their prayers favourably, great honour and wealth come to them.

l: riches and wealth, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 404-452) Again, Phoebe came to the desired embrace of Coeus.
s: Hecate bestows wealth upon those whose prayers she receives favourably. Her power is said to be responsible for this gift.

l: honour, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 404-452) Again, Phoebe came to the desired embrace of Coeus.
s: Hecate receives honour in starry heaven and from the deathless gods, and Zeus honours her above all. She also gives honour and glory to those whom she chooses, including victors in battle and contests.

l: nursing of the young, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 404-452) Again, Phoebe came to the desired embrace of Coeus.
s: Zeus makes Hecate a nurse of the young who, after that day, see the light of all-seeing Dawn. From the beginning, nursing the young is included among her honours.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: Rhea bears Zeus and, with the help of Earth and Heaven, conceals him in Crete while Cronos swallows a stone in his place and later regurgitates his children. Zeus frees the brothers of his father, receives the thunderbolt, defeats the Titans with the aid of Cottus, Gyes, and Briareos, and imprisons the Titans in Tartarus. Prometheus deceives Zeus at Mecone, steals fire for mortal men, and is punished, while Zeus has the Limping God create a maiden as an evil for humanity. The unit also describes the boundaries and inhabitants of Tartarus, including Night, Sleep, Death, Hades, Persephone, and Styx.

l: Rhea, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: Rhea bears Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, the Earth-Shaker, and Zeus to Cronos. When she is about to bear Zeus, she asks Earth and Heaven to conceal his birth, and they send her to Crete.

l: Cronos, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: Cronos swallows each child born to Rhea because he fears that one of his sons will take his kingship. Earth later deceives him, and he regurgitates his children after Zeus has grown strong.

l: Hades, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: Hades is one of the children whom Cronos swallows and later brings up again. He dwells beneath the earth, and his house with Persephone is guarded by a fearful hound.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: Zeus is concealed in Crete, grows quickly, and causes Cronos to restore his swallowed children. He frees the brothers of his father, receives the thunderbolt, leads the gods against the Titans, and rules over mortals and immortals.

l: Earth, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: Earth and Heaven devise the plan to conceal Zeus from Cronos. Earth receives Zeus in Crete, hides him in a cave, advises the gods to release the mighty brothers of their father, and helps bring about victory over the Titans.

l: Heaven, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: Heaven, together with Earth, tells Rhea what is destined to happen concerning Cronos and Zeus. Heaven is also described as a place from which a brazen anvil would take nine nights and days to reach Earth.

l: gods, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: The deathless gods fight the Titans for ten full years before Zeus brings the conflict to victory. They receive the aid of Cottus, Gyes, and Briareos, and they observe oaths sworn by the water of Styx.

l: men, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: Mortal men receive fire after Prometheus steals it from Zeus. They burn white ox-bones to the deathless gods, and Zeus makes the maiden as an evil for them; the text also describes marriage, women, children, poverty, and death as troubles among mortal men.

l: Iapetus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: Iapetus takes Clymene, daughter of Ocean, as his wife and fathers Atlas, Menoetius, Prometheus, and Epimetheus.

l: Atlas, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: Atlas is assigned by Zeus to uphold the wide heaven with his head and unwearied arms at the borders of the earth before the Hesperides.

l: Prometheus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: Prometheus deceives Zeus by dividing an ox so that the bones are covered with shining fat and the flesh is hidden under the paunch. He later steals fire for mortal men, is bound by Zeus, and has his liver eaten daily by an eagle until Heracles releases him.

l: Heracles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: Heracles, the son of Alcmene, kills the eagle that eats Prometheus's liver and releases Prometheus from his affliction. Zeus allows this so that Heracles's glory may become greater.

l: Pandora, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: The maiden associated with Pandora is formed from earth by the Limping God at Zeus's command as the price of fire. Athene clothes and adorns her, and she is presented to gods and men as an irresistible evil.

l: Cottus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: Cottus is bound beneath the earth by his father because of his great strength and size. Zeus and the other gods bring him back to the light, and he promises to fight the Titans before launching three hundred rocks against them.

l: Gyes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: Gyes is one of the mighty beings imprisoned beneath the earth by his father. After being released, he fights the Titans with Cottus and Briareos and later lives in Tartarus as a trusted warder of Zeus.

l: Briareos, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: Briareos is brought back from bondage beneath the earth and fights the Titans with Cottus and Gyes. He later dwells on Ocean's foundations, and the Earth-Shaker makes him his son-in-law by giving him Cymopolea.

l: Titans, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: The Titans fight Zeus and the gods for ten full years in a war whose outcome remains balanced until the mighty allies released by Zeus join the battle. They are defeated, bound, and hidden under the earth in Tartarus.

l: the Olympian gods, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: The gods associated with Olympus fight the Titan gods and receive the support of Cottus, Gyes, and Briareos. After their victory, they dwell on Olympus or in other divine places, while Zeus rules over the deathless gods.

l: Olympus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: Olympus is the place from which Zeus comes while hurling lightning against the Titans. It reels during the battle, and the gods who live in its house use the water of Styx for their oaths.

l: Tartarus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: Tartarus lies far beneath the earth and is separated by bronze gates, walls, gloom, and a vast gulf. The defeated Titans are imprisoned there, while Gyes, Cottus, and Obriareus serve as warders of Zeus.

l: Titanomachy, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: The Titanomachy lasts ten full years as the Titans and the gods born from Cronos fight for victory. Zeus's thunderbolts and the assaults of Cottus, Gyes, and Briareos finally turn the battle against the Titans.

l: the birth and concealment of Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: Rhea asks Earth and Heaven to hide Zeus's birth from Cronos. Earth carries him to Crete, places him in a remote cave on Mount Aegeum, and leaves Cronos a stone wrapped in swaddling clothes.

l: the swallowing and regurgitation of Cronos's children, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: Cronos swallows Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, the Earth-Shaker, and Zeus as they are born. After Zeus grows strong, Cronos is beguiled by Earth and vomits up the stone and then the children he had swallowed.

l: the release of the Cyclopes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: Zeus sets free the brothers of his father, the sons of Heaven whom Cronos had bound. In gratitude, they give Zeus the thunder, the glowing thunderbolt, and lightning.

l: the division of the ox at Mecone, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: At Mecone, Prometheus divides a great ox into portions for gods and mortal men. He hides the flesh under the paunch and covers the bones with fat, and Zeus's choice establishes the practice of burning white bones to the deathless gods.

l: fire, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: Zeus withholds unwearying fire from mortal men after Prometheus's deception. Prometheus steals its far-seen gleam in a hollow fennel stalk, and Zeus responds by creating an evil for men as its price.

l: Pandora's creation, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: At Zeus's command, the Limping God forms a maiden from earth. Athene clothes her in silvery raiment, adds a veil, garlands, and a golden crown, and the gods and men recognize her as an irresistible guile.

l: the punishment of Prometheus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: Zeus binds Prometheus with inextricable bonds and drives a shaft through his middle. A long-winged eagle eats his immortal liver each day, though it grows again at night, until Heracles kills the eagle and releases him with Zeus's consent.

l: thunderbolt, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: The brothers of Zeus's father give him the thunderbolt, thunder, and lightning after he releases them. Zeus uses the thunderbolt against the Titans, whose armies are overwhelmed by its fire, heat, and noise.

l: the stone given to Cronos, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: Earth gives Cronos a great stone wrapped in swaddling clothes instead of the newborn Zeus. Cronos swallows it, and Zeus later sets it in the earth at Pytho as a sign and marvel to mortal men.

l: the imprisonment of the Titans, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 453-491) But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid
s: After their defeat, the Titans are buried beneath the wide-pathed earth and bound in bitter chains. They are confined in Tartarus behind bronze gates and walls under the watch of Gyes, Cottus, and Obriareus.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 820-868) But when Zeus had driven the Titans from heaven, huge
s: Earth bears Typhoeus, her youngest child, who has immense strength, a hundred snake-headed necks, fiery eyes and heads, and many terrifying voices. Zeus confronts Typhoeus with thunder, lightning, and his thunderbolt, burns his heads, and hurls him into Tartarus after defeating him. The battle shakes heaven, earth, the sea, Olympus, Hades, and Tartarus, while the earth is scorched and melted by the heat. Winds come from Typhoeus; some are beneficial, but others damage ships, kill sailors, and ruin fields.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 820-868) But when Zeus had driven the Titans from heaven, huge
s: Zeus perceives the danger posed by Typhoeus and attacks him with thunder, lightning, and a lurid thunderbolt. He burns Typhoeus's heads, defeats him, and casts him into wide Tartarus.

l: Titans, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 820-868) But when Zeus had driven the Titans from heaven, huge
s: The Titans have been driven from heaven by Zeus. Those under Tartarus who live with Cronos tremble during the fearful strife between Zeus and Typhoeus.

l: Earth, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 820-868) But when Zeus had driven the Titans from heaven, huge
s: Earth bears Typhoeus as her youngest child. She groans during the battle, is scorched by the terrible vapour, and melts in the blazing fire.

l: Typhoeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 820-868) But when Zeus had driven the Titans from heaven, huge
s: Typhoeus is a hugely powerful monster with untiring feet, a hundred snake heads, flashing fire in his eyes and heads, and voices that imitate gods, bulls, lions, whelps, and hissing snakes. He threatens to rule mortals and immortals, but Zeus burns his heads, defeats him, and casts him into Tartarus.

l: Tartarus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 820-868) But when Zeus had driven the Titans from heaven, huge
s: Tartarus is the place into which Zeus casts the defeated Typhoeus. The Titans under Tartarus tremble during the unending clamour and fearful strife.

l: winds (from Typhoeus), Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 820-868) But when Zeus had driven the Titans from heaven, huge
s: Boisterous winds come from Typhoeus. Notus, Boreas, and clear Zephyr are god-sent and a great blessing to men, while the other winds blow fitfully.

l: Typhoeus's defeat, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 820-868) But when Zeus had driven the Titans from heaven, huge
s: Zeus's defeat of Typhoeus involves thunder, lightning, fire, and a thunderbolt that burns the monster's heads. Typhoeus is hurled down as a maimed wreck and then cast into Tartarus.

l: destructive winds, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 820-868) But when Zeus had driven the Titans from heaven, huge
s: Some winds from Typhoeus rush upon the sea, causing great havoc, scattering ships, and destroying sailors. Others sweep across the earth, filling fields with dust and cruel uproar and spoiling them.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 881-885) But when the blessed gods had finished their toil, and
s: The blessed gods ended their struggle with the Titans and pressed Olympian Zeus to rule, after which he distributed their dignities. Zeus swallowed Metis to prevent her prophesied son from challenging his rule, and later gave birth to Athene from his head. The unit recounts Zeus’s marriages and offspring, including Hera’s children, and the births and unions of many gods, heroes, and divine descendants. It ends with the Muses being asked to sing of the company of women.

l: gods, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 881-885) But when the blessed gods had finished their toil, and
s: The blessed gods finished their toil and settled their struggle for honours with the Titans by force. They pressed Olympian Zeus to reign and rule over them, and he divided their dignities among them.

l: Olympian Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 881-885) But when the blessed gods had finished their toil, and
s: Olympian Zeus was urged by the blessed gods, at Earth’s prompting, to reign over them and distribute their dignities. He married several goddesses, swallowed Metis to prevent her destined son from taking royal power, and gave birth to Athene from his own head. He also fathered numerous gods, heroes, and other children, including Apollo, Artemis, Hermes, Dionysus, and Heracles.

l: Metis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 881-885) But when the blessed gods had finished their toil, and
s: Metis was Zeus’s first wife and was described as the wisest among gods and mortal men. When she was about to bear Athene and a son destined to rule, Zeus deceived and swallowed her, placing her in his belly. She remained hidden within Zeus and continued to be associated with wisdom and the devising of good and evil.

l: Athena, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 881-885) But when the blessed gods had finished their toil, and
s: Athene was destined to be born as a very wise daughter of Metis, equal to her father in strength and understanding. Zeus gave birth to her from his head, and she emerged arrayed in the arms of war as a host-leading, battle-loving goddess.

l: Muses, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 881-885) But when the blessed gods had finished their toil, and
s: The nine gold-crowned Muses were born to Zeus and Mnemosyne, and they delight in feasts and the pleasures of song. At the end of the unit, they are asked to sing of the company of women.

l: Hera, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 881-885) But when the blessed gods had finished their toil, and
s: Hera became Zeus’s blooming wife and bore Hebe, Ares, and Eileithyia. In anger and quarrel with Zeus, she also bore Hephaestus without union with him.

l: Heracles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 881-885) But when the blessed gods had finished their toil, and
s: Heracles was born to Zeus and Alcmena and was called mighty and valiant. After completing his grievous labours, he married Hebe in Olympus and became deathless and unageing among the gods.

l: Olympus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 881-885) But when the blessed gods had finished their toil, and
s: Olympus is where the deathless gods dwell. Heracles lives there among the undying gods after completing his great works, and the Muses of Olympus are asked to sing.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CATALOGUES OF WOMEN AND EOIAE1701
s: This unit presents fragments attributed to Hesiod’s Catalogue of Women and related Catalogue genealogies, preserving genealogies, marriages, births, heroic exploits, and geographical traditions. It traces lines from Deucalion and Hellen, describes descendants of Zeus and Poseidon, and recounts stories involving Atalanta, Europa, Sarpedon, Phineus, Peleus, Thetis, and Asclepius. Several fragments concern the Argonauts, the Harpies, and distant peoples and places. The evidence comes from scholia, papyri, lexica, historians, and other later authors who quote or summarize Hesiod.

l: Hesiod, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CATALOGUES OF WOMEN AND EOIAE1701
s: Hesiod is cited as the author of genealogical and heroic material concerning gods, heroes, peoples, places, and marriages. The fragments attribute to him accounts of Deucalion’s descendants, the Argonauts and Harpies, Atalanta, Europa, Peleus and Thetis, and Asclepius, while also noting variant readings, interpolations, and works such as the Great Eoiae and the Journey round the Earth.

l: Catalogue of Women, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CATALOGUES OF WOMEN AND EOIAE1701
s: The Catalogue of Women is cited for genealogies and narratives including the descent of Deucalion, Hellen, Aeolus, the Argonauts, Atalanta, Europa, and the families of Peleus and Asclepius. The unit also distinguishes material from the first, second, and third Catalogues and from the Great Eoiae.

l: Deucalion, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CATALOGUES OF WOMEN AND EOIAE1701
s: Deucalion is identified as the son of Prometheus and Pronoea and as the father of Hellen by Pyrrha. His daughter Pandora bears Graecus to Zeus, and his daughter Thyia bears Magnes and Macedon to Zeus.

l: Hellen, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CATALOGUES OF WOMEN AND EOIAE1701
s: Hellen is identified as the son of Deucalion and Pyrrha. He is said to have fathered Dorus, Xuthus, and Aeolus.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CATALOGUES OF WOMEN AND EOIAE1701
s: Zeus fathers Graecus with Pandora, Magnes and Macedon with Thyia, and gives Endymion a special gift concerning the keeping of death. He carries Europa to Crete, fathers Minos, Rhadamanthys, and Sarpedon by her, and is invoked in accounts of Bellerophon, the Harpies, Aeacus, and the fate of Thetis.

l: Poseidon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CATALOGUES OF WOMEN AND EOIAE1701
s: Poseidon fathers Bellerophon with Eurynome, despite her being associated with Glaucus. He is also named as the father of the Aloiadae by Iphimedea, of Neleus and Pelias by Tyro, and of the twin sons of Actor and Molione.

l: Atalanta, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CATALOGUES OF WOMEN AND EOIAE1701
s: Atalanta is described as the beautiful, swift-footed daughter of Schoeneus who rejects marriage and competes in a deadly footrace. Hippomenes defeats her by casting three golden apples supplied through Aphrodite, allowing him to escape death and win her.

l: Europa, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CATALOGUES OF WOMEN AND EOIAE1701
s: Europa, the daughter of Phoenix, is carried from the mainland to Crete after Zeus deceives her in the form of a bull. She bears Minos, Rhadamanthys, and Sarpedon to Zeus.

l: Sarpedon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CATALOGUES OF WOMEN AND EOIAE1701
s: Sarpedon is one of the sons born to Europa and Zeus. He rules Lycia, receives honor and an extended life from Zeus, leads Lycian allies to Troy, fights beside Hector, and attacks the wall of the Danaans.

l: Phineus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CATALOGUES OF WOMEN AND EOIAE1701
s: Phineus is described in different Hesiodic traditions as the son of Phoenix and Cassiopea, or as having been blinded either for revealing the road to Phrixus or for choosing long life over sight. He has two sons, Thynus and Mariandynus, and is brought by the Harpies to the land of the milk-feeders.

l: Phrixus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CATALOGUES OF WOMEN AND EOIAE1701
s: Phrixus travels with Helle on an immortal ram with a golden fleece given to them by their mother Nephele. In one tradition, Phineus is blinded because he reveals the route to Phrixus.

l: Harpies, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CATALOGUES OF WOMEN AND EOIAE1701
s: The Harpies pursue or flee from the sons of Boreas across many lands and peoples. One Harpy falls into the river Tigris, while another reaches the Echinades, and the Harpies are not killed in the Hesiodic account; they also torment and transport Phineus.

l: Peleus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CATALOGUES OF WOMEN AND EOIAE1701
s: Peleus, the son of Aeacus, is involved in the account of Acastus’s attempt to have him killed by the Centaurs. He comes to Phthia with possessions from Iolcus and is celebrated for his marriage to a daughter of Nereus, identified elsewhere in the unit as Thetis.

l: Thetis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CATALOGUES OF WOMEN AND EOIAE1701
s: Thetis avoids marriage with Zeus in order to please Hera, and Zeus decrees that she must mate with a mortal. She consequently marries Peleus, and their marriage is celebrated as a divinely honored event.

l: Asclepius, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CATALOGUES OF WOMEN AND EOIAE1701
s: Asclepius is said in one tradition to be the son of Apollo and Arsinoe, and in another to be the son of Apollo and Coronis. The unit also gives a Hesiodic passage in which Arsinoe bears Asclepius and Eriopis to Apollo.

l: Catalogue genealogies, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CATALOGUES OF WOMEN AND EOIAE1701
s: The Catalogue genealogies preserve lines of descent among gods, heroes, kings, peoples, and places, including the families of Deucalion, Hellen, Aeolus, Lycaon, Europa, Aeacus, and Asclepius. They also record competing genealogical versions, such as different parentages for Phineus and Asclepius and differing accounts of the children of Amphion and Niobe.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #64—For how does he say that the same persons (the Cyclopes)
s: The text questions how the Cyclopes can be described as godlike yet also as destroyed by Apollo in the Catalogue of the Daughters of Leucippus. It states that Echemus made Timandra his wife. Hesiod is said to make Castor and Polydeuces both sons of Zeus. Hesiod also makes Helen the daughter of Ocean and Zeus, rather than of Leda or Nemesis.

l: Cyclopes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #64—For how does he say that the same persons (the Cyclopes)
s: The Cyclopes are described as being like the gods, yet they are also represented as being destroyed by Apollo.

l: Apollo, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #64—For how does he say that the same persons (the Cyclopes)
s: Apollo is represented as destroying the Cyclopes in the Catalogue of the Daughters of Leucippus.

l: Catalogue of the Daughters of Leucippus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #64—For how does he say that the same persons (the Cyclopes)
s: The Catalogue of the Daughters of Leucippus represents Apollo as destroying the Cyclopes.

l: Echemus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #64—For how does he say that the same persons (the Cyclopes)
s: Echemus made Timandra his buxom wife.

l: Timandra, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #64—For how does he say that the same persons (the Cyclopes)
s: Timandra was made the buxom wife of Echemus.

l: Hesiod, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #64—For how does he say that the same persons (the Cyclopes)
s: Hesiod makes Castor and Polydeuces both sons of Zeus. He also makes Helen the daughter of Ocean and Zeus, rather than of Leda or Nemesis.

l: Castor, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #64—For how does he say that the same persons (the Cyclopes)
s: Castor is presented by Hesiod as a son of Zeus.

l: Polydeuces, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #64—For how does he say that the same persons (the Cyclopes)
s: Polydeuces is presented by Hesiod as a son of Zeus.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #64—For how does he say that the same persons (the Cyclopes)
s: Zeus is presented as the father of Castor, Polydeuces, and Helen.

l: Helen, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #64—For how does he say that the same persons (the Cyclopes)
s: Hesiod makes Helen the daughter of Ocean and Zeus, not the child of Leda or Nemesis.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that
s: The unit preserves Hesiodic accounts of Helen’s suitors, Tyndareus’s oath, and the marriage of Helen and Menelaus, along with genealogies and episodes involving the gods and heroic families. Aphrodite punishes Tyndareus’s daughters for his neglect, while Zeus plans to destroy the demigods and separate gods from mortals. It also relates the Calydonian boar hunt, Meleager’s death at Apollo’s hands, and the descendants of Heracles, Amphiaraus, Electryon, Dardanus, and others. Later fragments concern Telephus, Dardanus, Ganymede, and Hyacinthus.

l: Hesiod, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that
s: Hesiod is cited for accounts of Aphrodite’s punishment of Tyndareus’s daughters, Helen’s suitors and marriage, the plans of Zeus concerning demigods, and numerous genealogies and heroic episodes. His Catalogue is also cited for Iphigeneia’s transformation into Hecate, the parentage of several figures, and stories involving the Calydonian boar, Heracles, and Dardanus.

l: Aphrodite, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that
s: Aphrodite became angry because Tyndareus forgot her while sacrificing to the gods. She caused his daughters to marry repeatedly and to desert their husbands, and she cast Timandra, Clytaemnestra, and Helen into evil report.

l: Tyndareus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that
s: Tyndareus forgot Aphrodite during a sacrifice, provoking her anger against his daughters. When Helen’s suitors came, he accepted none of their gifts, required them to swear an oath, and allowed Menelaus to prevail after Menelaus offered the greatest gifts.

l: Clytaemnestra, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that
s: Clytaemnestra deserted Agamemnon and lay with Aegisthus, choosing a worse mate.
